title: Age-dependent H3K9 trimethylation by dSetdb1 impairs mitochondrial UPR leading to degeneration of olfactory neurons and loss of olfactory function in Drosophila
abstract: Aging is characterized by a decline in essential sensory functions, including olfaction, which is crucial for environmental interaction and survival. This decline is often paralleled by the cellular accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria, particularly detrimental in post-mitotic cells such as neurons. Mitochondrial stress triggers the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRMT), a pathway that activates mitochondrial chaperones and antioxidant enzymes. Critical to the efficacy of the UPRMT is the cellular chromatin state, influenced by the methylation of lysine 9 on histone 3 (H3K9). While it has been observed that the UPRMT response can diminish with an increase in H3K9 methylation, its direct impact on age-related neurodegenerative processes, especially in the context of olfactory function, has not been clearly established. Using Drosophila, we demonstrate that an age-dependent increase in H3K9 trimethylation by the methyltransferase dSetdb1 reduces the activation capacity of the UPRMT in olfactory projection neurons leading to neurodegeneration and loss of olfactory function. Age-related neuronal degeneration was associated with morphological alterations in mitochondria and an increase in reactive oxygen species levels. Importantly, forced demethylation of H3K9 through knockdown of dSetdb1 in olfactory projection neurons restored the UPRMT activation capacity in aged flies, and suppressed age-related mitochondrial morphological abnormalities. This in turn prevented age-associated neuronal degeneration and rescued age-dependent loss of olfactory function. Our findings highlight the effect of age-related epigenetic changes on the response capacity of the UPRMT, impacting neuronal integrity and function. Moreover, they suggest a potential therapeutic role for UPRMT regulators in age-related neurodegeneration and loss of olfactory function.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This eLife article presents a convincing, landmark-level account of how age-dependent epigenetic change can weaken mitochondrial stress responses and contribute to olfactory neuron degeneration in Drosophila. The paper is published open access, includes linked peer-review materials, and has already been reused in one downstream Europe PMC article mention. The broader uptake record is still early, with no citations or public discussion captured yet.

Full narrative

The study addresses a central question in aging biology: why sensory function declines over time, and how mitochondrial dysfunction in neurons may be part of that process. According to the journal’s assessment, the work makes a convincing case that age-dependent H3K9 trimethylation by dSetdb1 impairs the mitochondrial unfolded protein response, leading to degeneration of olfactory neurons and loss of olfactory function. That framing gives the paper clear relevance across epigenetics, neurodegeneration, mitochondrion biology, and olfaction.

The publication context also supports visibility and reuse. It appears in eLife as a gold open-access article, with peer-review files published alongside the paper, which improves transparency and makes the research easier to evaluate and teach from. The record also shows one documented downstream reuse in Europe PMC, indicating at least limited scholarly uptake beyond the original article.

Funding support is substantial and multi-source, drawing on several Chilean research and infrastructure awards, including multiple Fondo Nacional de Desarrollo Científico y Tecnológico grants, a center-based funding award, an ANID installation grant, and basal support for Centro Ciencia and Vida. This suggests the work is embedded in a sustained research program rather than a one-off project.

At the same time, the observable engagement record remains sparse. The digest reports zero OpenAlex citations, zero scite citations, and no captured event data or public discourse, so the article’s longer-term scholarly and public reach is still unfolding. In other words, the publication is strong on scientific significance and transparency, while its citation trajectory has yet to develop in the available record.

Overall, this is a well-supported open-access contribution that connects chromatin regulation to age-related sensory decline in a model system. Its strongest signal is conceptual: it offers a mechanistic explanation for how epigenetic changes can compromise neuronal resilience during aging.
